question: At autopsy of a suspected insulin homicide, post-mortem blood glucose is normal. Which investigation would BEST confirm exogenous insulin administration?

answers.text: Post-mortem C-peptide measurement (high insulin:C-peptide ratio confirms exogenous source)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Endogenous insulin is always secreted with C-peptide (proinsulin cleavage product) in equimolar amounts. Commercial insulin contains NO C-peptide. A high insulin:C-peptide ratio (high insulin, absent/low C-peptide) is forensic proof of exogenous insulin administration.

Insufficient alone. Post-mortem insulin levels cannot distinguish endogenous from exogenous sources by concentration alone. The insulin:C-peptide ratio is required. Additionally, post-mortem insulin release from decomposing pancreatic cells can elevate insulin levels artificially.

Incorrect. Post-mortem glucose levels normalise rapidly due to glycogenolysis and are unreliable. Urine glucose would reflect ante-mortem metabolism, not a specific indicator of exogenous insulin. C-peptide is the forensic anchor.

Incorrect. Pancreatic histology would be normal in exogenous insulin injection — the injected insulin comes from outside, not from islet cell disease. Histology cannot identify exogenous insulin administration.

overallFeedback.feedback: C-peptide is the correct answer. Post-mortem glucose is unreliable (normalises quickly). Total insulin alone is non-specific. Only the insulin:C-peptide ratio distinguishes endogenous secretion (both present) from exogenous injection (insulin high, C-peptide absent/low).

Correct. The insulin:C-peptide ratio is the definitive forensic test for insulin homicide. Normal: insulin and C-peptide rise proportionally (both from proinsulin). Exogenous insulin injection: high insulin, absent C-peptide. This is also used in factitious hypoglycaemia investigation.
